design_detail: Narrative review of structural MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, PET and SPECT (dopamine and serotonin transporters, VMAT2, D2/D3 receptors, translocator protein, glucose metabolism, blood flow), MR spectroscopy, task fMRI and resting-state fMRI studies in people who use methamphetamine, with sections linking the findings to executive function and to treatment. No methods section: no search strategy, inclusion criteria, appraisal of cited studies or quantitative synthesis. Four figures, three of them from studies first-authored by co-authors of the review (Morales et al., 2012; Kohno et al., 2014) and one from a monkey study (Groman et al., 2013).
can_establish: Which neuroimaging findings the authors considered central in 2014 and which primary studies a reader should check for each marker.
cannot_establish: That the imaging differences it describes are caused by methamphetamine, how large or consistent they are across studies, or whether they and the associated cognitive differences recover with abstinence, because it has no systematic search, no appraisal of the cited studies and no synthesis, and most of the studies it cites are small and cross-sectional.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: narrative review of published studies chosen by the authors; no search, sources or dates reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported. The abstract defines the scope as structural, molecular and functional neuroimaging studies, with a focus on cortical and striatal abnormalities.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Sample sizes and abstinence durations are given for only a few cited studies (for example 5 users in each of two DAT recovery studies; 13 vs 27 users in a blood-flow study).
sample.selection_effects: Selection of studies is by the authors, with no stated criteria. Three of four figures come from studies first-authored by co-authors (Morales et al., 2012; Kohno et al., 2014), and two cited sources are unpublished conference presentations (Ballard et al., 2014; Robertson et al., 2013). The reference list does not include Hart et al. (2012), the critical review of whether cognition is impaired in people who use methamphetamine, while it does include Dean et al. (listed as 2012).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). Exposure measurement in the cited studies is not described.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed for cigarette smoking only: smoking is reported in 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine against 22% of the general population, and a cited study found smaller orbitofrontal and caudate grey matter in smokers with and without methamphetamine use (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th paragraph). Polydrug use is noted as a limitation of one D3 receptor study (Boileau et al., 2012). Alcohol, cannabis and other drug use in the cited studies are not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Reported study by study where relevant; ranges cited run from 4–10 days to 25 years of abstinence.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (review). Cited studies compare users with non-users; matching is described only as 'matched' for the DAT studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review raises premorbid and familial explanations itself: brain structure and addiction are both heritable, and in a sibling study (Ersche et al., 2012) stimulant-dependent people and their siblings without drug use shared some differences from controls (larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampus; lower fractional anisotropy) (Structural Brain Imaging, 7th paragraph). It does not apply this reasoning to the molecular or functional findings.

outcomes.instruments: Grey-matter volume and density (MRI), fractional anisotropy (DTI), DAT ([11C]WIN-35,428, [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate, [99mTc]TRODAT), SERT ([11C](+)McN-5652), VMAT2 ([11C]dihydrotetrabenazine), D2/D3 receptors ([11C]raclopride, [18F]fallypride, [11C]-(+)-PHNO), translocator protein ([11C]PK11195), NAA, choline, creatine, myo-inositol and glutamate (MRS), glucose metabolism ([18F]FDG), blood flow ([99mTc]HMPAO), task and resting-state fMRI.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Deficit' and 'dysfunction' denote a group difference from non-users in an imaging marker, or a correlation of a marker with a task score; no study's effect size or normative comparison is given for cognition.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the review. Of its own figures, Figure 1 is shown at p<0.005 uncorrected with a 200-voxel cluster extent; Figures 2–4 are reported as corrected.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no effect sizes for cognitive outcomes. Numbers cited: striatal DAT 11–28% lower in abstinent users than matched non-users across six PET studies; DAT increases of up to 38% in the first two weeks of abstinence in 5 users (Chou et al., 2007) and of 19% (caudate) and 16% (putamen) between early (<6 months) and later (12–17 months) abstinence in 5 users (Volkow et al., 2001b); striatal VMAT2 22%, 12% and 11% higher in early abstinence (Boileau et al., 2008) but 10% lower after more than 3 months (Johanson et al., 2006); striatal D2-type receptor availability 16% (caudate), 13% (putamen) and 8% (nucleus accumbens) lower in users abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months (Monoamine systems, 2nd–4th paragraphs).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. The figures from the authors' own fMRI work are reported as controlled for age, sex, smoking and cannabis use (Figures 3–4 legends).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; no methods section.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is selected without stated criteria. The review cites Chou et al. (2007) as preliminary evidence that executive function recovers with DAT recovery, without the caveat raised in Simon et al. (2010), which shares its senior author, that Chou et al. had no control group for WCST practice effects. Simon et al. (2010) is cited only as support for common executive deficits, not for its null result on cognitive change over the first month. Hart et al. (2012) is not cited.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The body describes group differences from non-users in many imaging markers, mostly from small cross-sectional studies; concedes that human studies generally cannot attribute structural abnormalities to methamphetamine (Structural Brain Imaging, 6th paragraph); offers smoking and familial vulnerability as explanations for some structural findings (paragraphs 4 and 7); and supports recovery with abstinence by within-person changes in samples of about 5 or by a one-month grey-matter change shown at an uncorrected threshold.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract present corticostriatal deficits of chronic use and state that users "often display several signs of corticostriatal dysfunction" linked to addiction-related phenotypes (Abstract), without mentioning confounding by smoking, premorbid or familial differences, or polydrug use. The white-matter findings are called consistent with drug-induced damage (Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph). The Introduction cites Simon et al. (2010) for common executive-function deficits, although that study found no significant executive difference and placed users' mean scores in the low-average to average range (see sc_simon_2010). A paragraph heading claim that cortical grey-matter deficits reverse with protracted abstinence rests on one month of abstinence (Figure 1, uncorrected) and a cross-sectional comparison (Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph). The treatment suggestions (anti-inflammatory drugs, exercise, D3 targets, cognitive remediation) are presented as possibilities and rest on animal or preliminary data.

timeline.event: DAT follow-up in 5 users (19% and 16% increases), cited by this review as Volkow et al., 2001b.
Thalamic metabolic recovery at 12–17 months in 5 users, cited by this review as associated with motor and verbal memory improvement.

Simon et al. (2010): no significant executive-function difference after about 6 days of abstinence and no significant differential cognitive change over a month against retested controls; cited by this review only for cognitive deficits.
Sibling study of stimulant dependence, cited for structural differences shared with unaffected siblings.
Critical review of whether cognition is impaired in people who use methamphetamine; not cited by this review.
Evaluation of the evidence that methamphetamine causes cognitive decline; cited by this review as Dean et al., 2012.

replication.where_it_stands: Useful as a map of imaging markers and their primary sources, each of which needs its own card. On the encyclopedia's questions it adds no independent evidence: causation is conceded to be unresolved for structural findings, magnitudes are given only as percentage differences in transporter and receptor binding, and the recovery evidence it cites consists of very small within-person studies.

funding.funder: Endowment from the Thomas P and Katherine K Pike Chair in Addiction Studies and a gift from the Marjorie M Greene Trust (EDL); T32 DA 024635 (MEB), F31 DA0331-17 (AMM), F31 DA033120-02 (MK) (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the PMC author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at UCLA (Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences; also Molecular and Medical Pharmacology and the Brain Research Institute for the first author). The review relies in part on the authors' own studies. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the review's own question, a registered systematic review that pools user–control differences marker by marker, codes smoking, polydrug use and abstinence for every study, and keeps within-person longitudinal evidence separate from cross-sectional comparisons; for causation, imaging cohorts that begin before regular use, or methamphetamine-specific discordant-sibling designs, with controls scanned at the same intervals.

domains.note: There is no methods section: no databases, dates or selection criteria are reported, and only the scope (structural, molecular and functional imaging, focused on cortical and striatal abnormalities) is stated (Abstract).

There is no appraisal of the cited studies as such; limitations are named for some findings (smoking and familial explanations for structural data, polydrug use in Boileau et al., 2012, conflicting VMAT2 results; Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs; Monoamine systems, 3rd and 5th paragraphs). The recovery evidence (two DAT studies of 5 users each; Figure 1 at p<0.005 uncorrected) is presented without comment on size or threshold (Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph; Monoamine systems, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Six of the 142 bibliography entries name a review author (Ballard 2014, a poster; Kohno 2013, 2014; London 2004; Morales 2012; Payer 2011), and at least six 'et al.' entries are from the senior author's group by the author lists printed in Hart et al. (2012) and Dean et al. (2013) (e.g., Lee 2009, Monterosso 2005, Simon 2010). These supply 3 of the 4 figures, the grey-matter recovery claim, the risky decision-making and resting-state findings, and 3 of the 4 citations for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

The abstract presents group differences as corticostriatal 'dysfunction' without the body's caveats that human studies cannot assign structural differences to methamphetamine and that smoking or familial factors may explain some (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs). The claim that grey-matter deficits reverse with protracted abstinence rests on one month of abstinence shown at an uncorrected threshold (3rd paragraph; Figure 1), and lower fractional anisotropy is read as drug-induced damage in the 5th paragraph and as familial predisposition in the 7th.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against methamphetamine-caused brain and cognitive deficits
domains.note: Under-represented: evidence that the functional and cognitive differences are small, absent or not caused by methamphetamine; counter-evidence is given for structural findings (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs) and a few molecular ones (Monoamine systems, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs) but not for these. Hart et al. (2012) is not in the bibliography, and Simon et al. (2010), listed with no significant differences in Dean et al. (2013, Table 1), is cited only for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because there is no search or selection method, the abstract and section-level claims go beyond the evidence and caveats the body itself gives, and a notable share of the evidence comes from the authors' group. It may be cited as a pointer to primary imaging studies marker by marker, and for its own statement that human studies cannot attribute structural differences to methamphetamine. It may not be cited as evidence of methamphetamine-caused deficits, of recovery with abstinence, or of common executive-function deficits.

key_findings.finding: The review has no methods section: no search, inclusion criteria, appraisal or synthesis is reported.
The authors state that human studies generally do not allow structural abnormalities to be assigned to methamphetamine use itself and turn to animal studies for that question.
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In vervet monkeys given an escalating methamphetamine regimen, putamen grey matter increased (p<0.05 corrected), together with lower D2-type receptor and DAT availability and poorer cognitive flexibility (Groman et al., 2013, as summarized).
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging, 6th paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The review describes the regimen as resembling a common pattern of human use ('escalating' comes from the Figure 2 title) and presents the D2-type receptor and DAT reductions as associated with the grey-matter increase; it gives no magnitudes and no data on persistence. Elsewhere it cites recovery of D2-type receptor availability with protracted abstinence in monkeys (Groman et al., 2012; Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Cigarette smoking is reported in 87–92% of people who use methamphetamine against 22% of the general population; in a cited study, smokers with and without methamphetamine use had smaller orbitofrontal and caudate grey matter than non-smoking non-users, so those deficits may partly reflect smoking or premorbid conditions.

In a sibling study of 50 cocaine- or amphetamine-dependent people, dependent people and their non-using siblings both had larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampus and lower fractional anisotropy than controls; only the dependent people had smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes. The review concludes some but not all structural differences may predate drug use.
key_findings.note: The review gives no effect sizes, no breakdown of the 50 dependent participants by drug, and no sibling-versus-control comparison of inhibitory control; the next section reports only that fractional anisotropy near the right inferior frontal gyrus went with stop-signal performance across all three groups (Deficits in Brain Structure and Impaired Executive Functions, 1st paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Grey matter increased in several cortical regions between the first and fourth week of abstinence in users, with no change in controls scanned a month apart; the figure is thresholded at p<0.005 uncorrected with a 200-voxel cluster extent.
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Striatal DAT was 11–28% lower in abstinent users than in matched non-users across six PET studies; DAT rose by up to 38% in the first two weeks in 5 users (SPECT) and by 19% (caudate) and 16% (putamen) between early and later abstinence in 5 users (PET).
DAT availability correlated with cognitive or psychomotor performance in some studies (McCann et al., 2008; Volkow et al., 2001d) but not in another (Johanson et al., 2006).

Striatal VMAT2 was higher than controls in early abstinence (+22% caudate, +12% putamen, +11% ventral striatum) in one study and 10% lower after more than 3 months in another; a post-mortem study found no difference.

Striatal D2-type receptor availability was 16% (caudate), 13% (putamen) and 8% (nucleus accumbens) lower in users abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months; the authors state that no human study has followed D2-type receptors over abstinence.
key_findings.note: Cited to Volkow et al., 2001b, which in the review's own reference list is the DAT recovery paper (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: MRS markers of neuronal integrity (NAA/creatine in anterior cingulate) are lower in users and are described as recovering slowly with extended abstinence; one PET study found more translocator-protein binding in users, lower with longer abstinence.

Lower right anterior cingulate blood flow was found in 13 users abstinent a mean 3 months (SD 2) than in 27 abstinent a mean 36 months (SD 40), taken as a sign of recovery (cross-sectional comparison).
The review cites Simon et al. (2010), among others, for the statement that cognitive deficits, particularly in executive functions, are common in people with a history of methamphetamine use.
key_findings.note: Simon et al. (2010) found no significant executive-function difference (sc_simon_2010).

key_findings.finding: Dopamine agonists (modafinil, methylphenidate, d-amphetamine) are described as not consistently efficacious; anti-inflammatory drugs, exercise, D3-receptor targets and cognitive remediation are proposed as possibilities on animal or preliminary evidence.

The review states that people who use methamphetamine generally have smaller cortical but larger striatal grey-matter volumes than people who do not. After under 3 weeks of abstinence, anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal, superior temporal and hippocampal volumes were smaller than in people who never used it (Nakama et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2004), with an insular density deficit at up to 6 months of abstinence (Schwartz et al., 2010); people abstinent a mean 3–4 months had larger parietal, caudate, lenticular and accumbens volumes (Jernigan et al., 2005) and larger putamen and globus pallidus (Chang et al., 2005), and putamen volume was also larger in people still using (Jan et al., 2012b).
key_findings.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand summaries of cross-sectional studies; the primary papers have not been read.

key_findings.finding: In places the authors lean toward neurotoxicity: they open the neuronal-integrity section by citing mounting evidence (reviews, largely of animal work) that repeated exposure can be neurotoxic, and suggest that dopamine agonists may have failed partly because of methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity to dopamine nerve terminals, while their own summary reports partial DAT recovery with abstinence, inconsistent VMAT2 findings and no human longitudinal data on D2-type receptors.
key_findings.locator: Molecular Imaging › Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, 1st paragraph; Implications for Therapy, 2nd paragraph; Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 2nd–4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: An interpretation, hedged by the authors (agonist failure 'may in part' reflect neurotoxicity); no human study of terminal counts is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The D2 receptor findings (raclopride binding 16%, 13% and 8% lower; correlation with orbitofrontal metabolism) are cited to Volkow et al., 2001b, but the reference list assigns 2001b to the Journal of Neuroscience DAT recovery paper; the D2/orbitofrontal paper is listed as 2001a.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph; Bibliography
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone tracing these numbers must use the American Journal of Psychiatry 2001;158:2015–21 paper, not the DAT recovery paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The only Kim et al. (2006) entry in the reference list is titled as a study of prefrontal grey-matter changes, yet Kim et al. (2006) is cited for grey-matter density, WCST errors, a correlation of executive deficits with fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum, and lower white-matter glucose metabolism in users abstinent 19 months (SD 27).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Deficits in Brain Structure, 2nd paragraph; Regional Brain Function, 4th paragraph; Bibliography
reporting_issues.consequence: The diffusion and metabolism attributions cannot be matched to the listed source; check the primary paper before any claim relies on them. Hart et al. (2012, Table 2, p. 594) list the white-matter glucose finding in men abstinent 19 (SD 27) months under Kim et al. (2005), so that part is probably a miscitation of the 2005 study.

reporting_issues.issue: Users are said to have lower fractional anisotropy in the genu of the corpus callosum, but Stroop and WCST deficits are said to correlate with increased fractional anisotropy in the genu.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph; Deficits in Brain Structure, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the structure–cognition relation is stated inconsistently; the primary studies (Salo et al., 2009a) must be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: A paragraph that opens by saying glucose metabolism remains abnormal throughout protracted abstinence cites mixed evidence: a prefrontal white-matter deficit at a mean 19 months of abstinence (attributed to Kim et al., 2006) and the absence of a striatal increase at 12–17 months fit the opening, while a thalamic increase at 12–17 months that went with better motor and verbal-memory performance (Wang et al., 2004) and higher anterior cingulate blood flow with longer abstinence (Hwang et al., 2006) point to partial recovery.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Regional Brain Function, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The opening sentence overstates persistence: the paragraph's own evidence shows persisting differences in some measures and partial recovery in others.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction cites Simon et al. (2010) as support for common executive-function deficits; that study found a significant difference on one processing-speed test only, none in executive domains, and none after adjusting for education.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation overstates its source; claims should cite primary data, not this sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the listed training grants is printed as F31 DA0331-17, which appears truncated.

London et al. (2004) is cited for poorer sustained attention among recently abstinent users that correlated negatively with metabolism in the anterior and middle cingulate and the insula (Regional Brain Function, 2nd paragraph). Hart et al. (2012) report that the groups in London et al. (2004) did not differ on task performance (p. 597) and place the attention deficit and these correlations in London et al. (2005; Table 2, p. 595), which is not in this review's bibliography.
reporting_issues.consequence: The attention finding belongs to London et al. (2005) and should be checked there; the 2004 study found no performance difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Salo et al. (2009a) is cited for lower fractional anisotropy in the genu of the corpus callosum in users (Structural Brain Imaging, 5th paragraph). Hart et al. (2012) report that in that study the groups did not differ on any DTI measure and that slower Stroop responses went with lower genu fractional anisotropy regardless of group (p. 601).
reporting_issues.consequence: The genu difference attributed to Salo et al. (2009a) is not supported by Hart's account, and the correlation runs with lower, not higher, fractional anisotropy (compare the issue on the direction of the genu correlation); check the primary paper before citing either.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 3 (2026-10-16): editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high; domains: Systematic search and explicit selection: high; Appraisal of cited studies: some-concerns; Reliance on the authors' own studies: some-concerns; Separation of evidence from speculation: high; Balance of evidence for and against methamphetamine-caused brain and cognitive deficits: some-concerns
disagreements.resolution: Applied (METHODS §5.3). Pending a check of the new domain judgments by a second reader or the senior author.

disagreements.first_pass: issue: A paragraph that opens by saying glucose metabolism remains abnormal throughout protracted abstinence goes on to cite evidence of increases and signs of recovery (thalamic increase at 12–17 months; higher blood flow with longer abstinence).; consequence: The paragraph's lead claim is not what its evidence shows.
disagreements.reviewer: Corrected: the evidence is mixed rather than contrary. The striatal non-recovery (Wang et al., 2004) and the prefrontal white-matter deficit at 19 months (attributed to Kim et al., 2006) support the opening sentence; only the thalamic increase and the blood-flow comparison point to recovery. The sentence overstates persistence somewhat but is not contradicted by its evidence.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Regional Brain Function, 4th paragraph: two of the four findings fit the opening sentence and two point to partial recovery. Issue and consequence rewritten to describe mixed evidence.

Checked while adjudicating the matching anchor (cl_meth_dopamine_damage, anchor 13): how the regimen is described and the association framing matter for a claim about use as people use it. Note added; finding unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed (for cl_meth_siblings): the review gives no sibling-versus-control comparison of inhibitory control (only a fractional anisotropy–stop-signal correlation across all three groups) and no cocaine/amphetamine split of the 50 dependent participants; those parts need the primary paper (Ersche et al., 2012).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Structural Brain Imaging, 7th paragraph, and Deficits in Brain Structure and Impaired Executive Functions, 1st paragraph. Added as a note so that cl_meth_siblings does not cite this review for points it does not contain.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: larger striatal and parietal grey-matter volumes in users than non-users (Berman 2008a; Jernigan 2005; Chang 2005; Jan 2012b; Structural Brain Imaging, 2nd paragraph); relevant to how cl_meth_grey_matter frames the structural literature.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Structural Brain Imaging, 2nd paragraph. Added because cl_meth_grey_matter now cites this paragraph for the larger striatal and parietal volumes.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the causal neurotoxicity framing of the dopamine findings (Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, 1st paragraph; Implications for Therapy, 2nd paragraph) is recorded neither among key findings nor in the interpretation gap; it matters for cl_meth_dopamine_damage.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed at both places. Added as a key finding because cl_meth_dopamine_damage cites this review; the interpretation-gap text is unchanged (left to the senior author).
